verdict.reasoning: Patient states: “my knees are hurting and they're clicking a lot… I can't run very far anymore without just feeling pain in my knees… I'm just concerned and I figured… see if you can help me figure out what's going on.” Later clarifies it is the right knee.
Duration: “probably it's been about two weeks.” Trigger: increased running for marathon training. Clicking: “now my knees are hurting and they're clicking a lot,” later specified as right knee.

Current distance: “maybe like seven or eight miles.” Prior: “I've done like, you know, four or five miles and I've just done like a couple of seven mile runs.” Weekly frequency is not specified but the distance progression is.
“I would say it probably starts like after maybe 20 minutes or so, which is probably, I don't know, like somewhere around mile three, maybe and a half or three miles.”
“When I do my abs, it kind of requires me… to go from the flex position of my knees and straighten my legs. Then I hear all this clicking.”
Patient describes clicking associated with the knee during movement/ab exercises and earlier says knees are “clicking a lot.” Right side later specified: “It's actually my right knee that hurts.”
When asked about giving way: Patient explains the concept then says: “Not that. I mean, it just kind of starts hurting, you know.”
When asked: “Any locking up of the knee? No, can't straighten it. Any problems going up and down stairs?” Patient answers: “No.”
“Well, it did. Like, the first time I ran, it was a little bit swollen, but then I just put some, like, ice on it and it went away.” Refers to the symptomatic (right) knee.
“But right now, right now it's not swollen.”
“Right now it doesn't hurt, you know, but it just kind of comes on when… when I run, it will start hurting.”
Range of motion: Patient answers “Yes” to both “are you able to fully straighten the leg?” and “what about fully flex it?”
“There was this tingling in my toes. Like, after the run, there was tingling in my toes, like, on my… my right toes.” She also notes it occurred once (“I felt this just once”).
“I do have. I'm farsighted and so I had. I had LASIK surgery.”
“Once I had this really bad uti. They thought it was kidney stones, and so they had me actually in er…”
“Well, I had, you know, just kind of your garden variety stuff. Right. Colds and… But other than that, you know, I'm… I'm pretty good.”
“Yes, I take ibuprofen and I'll just kind of use it sometime… maybe like 400 milligrams max.”
“I'll take like, ibuprofen or actually acetamin. I'll take. What am I taking? Aleve.” This indicates acetaminophen use.
“I'll take like, ibuprofen or actually acetamin. I'll take. What am I taking? Aleve.” Aleve is naproxen.
“I take melatonin sometimes.”
“Well, I'll take. I take vitamin D.”
“Occasionally if I'm really having hard times, like I'll sleeping, I'll take Xanax, but I prefer melatonin.”
No allergies are mentioned anywhere in the transcript; stating that no drug allergies are noted reflects absence of documentation.
“I'm currently training for a marathon that's going to happen in June.”
“I also sometimes will, you know, smoke a joint.”
Tobacco use is not discussed at all; stating no significant tobacco use is effectively noting it is not documented.
Alcohol use is not mentioned anywhere; stating no alcohol use details are provided matches the transcript.
“Right now it doesn't hurt… but… when I run, it will start hurting.” Indicates activity-related pain.
“The first time I ran, it was a little bit swollen, but then… I put some… ice on it and it went away.”
Transcript mentions future red-flag symptoms including heat/redness but does not state that the patient currently has no warmth or redness of the knee.
Denies giving way: “Not that.” Denies locking: “Any locking up of the knee?... Any problems going up and down stairs? – No.”
Full ROM confirmed: “are you able to fully straighten the leg?” – “Yes.” “what about fully flex it?” – “Yes.”
“There was this tingling in my toes… after the run… on my… my right toes.”
“And with your foot, has that gone back to normal now? Do you feel any altered sensation, tingling, numbness…? – No, it was just. It was that time.” So no persistent numbness.

When asked about other joints/back/etc., she only mentions occasional leg/foot swelling and toe tingling; no other joint pains reported: “Any other joint problems…? – Well, I have sometimes… legs will swell up… Another weird thing… tingling in my toes.” No additional joint pain.
No vitals (BP, HR, temp, etc.) are mentioned in the transcript.
This is a teleconsultation; there is no described physical examination, only history questions and patient self-report.
“Right now it's not swollen.”

No statement is made about current warmth or erythema of the knee; only general question about lower leg color/temperature (“Any change in color or temperature of your lower legs? – Nope.”), not knee-specific warmth/redness.
“Are you able to fully straighten the leg? – Yes… what about fully flex it? – Yes.”

Pain with running: “when I run, it will start hurting.” Pain/clicking with flexion–extension during abs: “when I do my abs… go from the flex position… and straighten my legs. Then I hear all this clicking.”
Patient self-reports prior swelling and suspects fluid: “Well, I have probably some fluid. I googled it… does the knee look swollen?… it was a little bit swollen… then… it went away.”
Patient is asked about tenderness: “Have you noticed any tenderness…?” She responds by talking about fluid and swelling; she does not affirm tenderness to palpation.
Clicking described with movement: “now my knees are hurting and they're clicking a lot” and during abs exercises “Then I hear all this clicking.”
“After the run, there was tingling in my toes… on my right toes.”
“Any change in color or temperature of your lower legs? – Nope.”
Denies instability/giving way: “Not that.” Denies locking: “Any locking up of the knee?... Any problems going up and down stairs? – No.”
History shows overuse from marathon training, right knee pain with running and mechanical clicking, full ROM, and explicit denial of instability and locking, consistent with this summary.
Transcript notes right toe tingling once and that it resolved; there is no clinician statement that it is “likely benign but requiring monitoring.” That interpretive assessment is not documented.

Plan: continue ice, reduce running, prescribe stronger anti-inflammatory, refer to physiotherapist, consider imaging after assessment—this is a conservative management plan with physio and conditional imaging.
“What I would suggest is definitely carrying on with the ice therapy that you've been using. So as much as you can…”

“I would try and ease up on the running if you can. And if it's painful enough that you're having to stop running, then it's not a good idea to do that.” This implies avoiding pain‑provoking mileage and adjusting as tolerated.

“It's fine to take the ibuprofen. I can prescribe you a slightly stronger anti inflammatory that you can take regularly instead of the ibuprofen, but not with the ibuprofen, but make sure that with food.”
The doctor does not mention continuing acetaminophen or other OTC analgesics explicitly, nor discuss overlapping NSAID use beyond saying not to take the new anti-inflammatory with ibuprofen.

“Ultimately, we probably need to examine the knee. So the best thing, I would suggest getting an appointment with the physiotherapist first. You can do like a long assessment and examination of the knee…”

“Then make an assessment as to whether we need to do any imagery to have a look inside the knee and see if there's any problem with the cartilage.” Imaging is proposed if needed after physio assessment and persistent concerns.

“If in the meantime you develop like persistent swelling, heat, redness of the knee or high temperature, feel unwell, or it completely locks up and you can't bend and stretch it, then you'd need to see a doctor urgently.”

Regarding ACL concern: “It's not really possible to diagnose that over the phone, over the video. So we definitely would need to see you.” This conveys that ligament injury requires in-person exam/imaging.
No specific follow-up interval such as “1–2 weeks” is given; the only timing is to call back or see a doctor urgently if red-flag symptoms develop.
